inline.s: [Thus, at the place where the mind stirs and a thought arises, test it with forbearance; at the place where the foot steps and the body moves, let forbearance go before; at the place of turning and of countenance, uphold it with forbearance; at the place of joy and anger, sorrow and pleasure, verify it with forbearance. Doing so, the mind will not dare to stir recklessly, the body will not dare to act recklessly, affairs will not dare to be undertaken recklessly, and the feelings will not dare to go forth recklessly. Hence Laozi said: “Not daring to be first in the world.” “Not daring” is but another name for forbearance. Because of “not daring to be first in the world,” forbearance is the foremost practice for attaining Buddhahood.]

Therefore, at the place where the mind stirs and a thought arises, examine it with forbearance (surrender to the present moment); at the place where the foot steps and the body moves, let forbearance (surrender to the present moment) lead the way; in dealing with people and receiving things, respond with forbearance (surrender to the present moment); at the place of joy, anger, sorrow, and pleasure, verify it with forbearance (surrender to the present moment). Doing so, the mind will not dare to stir recklessly, the body will not dare to act recklessly, affairs will not dare to be undertaken recklessly, and the feelings will not dare to go forth recklessly. Hence Laozi’s Daode Jing says: “Not daring to act willfully (following one’s own nature) is to be the foremost one in the world.” “Not daring” is but another name for forbearance. And because not daring (forbearance) is to be the foremost in the world, forbearance is the most essential practice (the foremost practice) for attaining Buddhahood.
[Zhe xuan: deportment, bearing.] [Dong rong: a facial expression appears.]

[Thus forbearance is great while self is small. Therefore forbearance can be a garment to cover me, and can also be a garment to cover all things; there is no virtue of self-benefit and benefiting others beyond it. Hence it is said that gentleness and forbearance are a garment—that is why. A Chan practitioner came seeking a word of Dharma, so I entitled this: Forbearance as Attire. Practitioner, strive to practice it—do not make of it mere idletalk, and do not use it as a means to buy food and livelihood.]

Thus forbearance is great while self is small. Therefore forbearance can shelter me as a warm garment shelters one in the depth of winter, and can also shelter others; there is no virtue of self-benefit and benefiting others that surpasses forbearance. Hence it is said that one must take gentleness and forbearance as a garment—this is the meaning of it! The Chan practitioner Fajin came seeking a word of Dharma, so I entitled this instruction: Forbearance as Attire. Fajin, you must strive and practice it! Do not suppose this is a worn-out commonplace, and do not use it as a means to gain reputation and material benefit.

[Ren ru yi (forbearance as a garment): the mind of forbearance can guard against all external hindrances, so it is likened to a garment.] [Kou tou hua: the stock phrases that stay ever upon one’s lips.] [Bo: to exchange.] [Do not use it to buy food and livelihood] Master Hanshan here earnestly admonishes: to study and grasp the principle one must practice it personally; do not fail to practice it yourself and yet use it to teach others as a means to gain reputation and material benefit. The Analects

Xianwen chapter says: “The learning of the ancients was for oneself; the learning of today is for others.” The Analects Commentary and Sub-commentary says: “The ancients studied and then practiced it—this was for oneself. People today can only speak it for others, unable to practice it themselves—this is for others. Fan Ye said: ‘The one who is for others relies on praise to make himself known; the one who is for himself follows his own mind and meets the Way.’” [Feng yu yi xian wu (relying on praise to make oneself known): to rely on reputation to appear before others—that is, to fish for fame and praise.] “Feng” was in ancient times the same as “ping,” to rely on, to depend upon. “Wu” means people other than oneself.
